THOUGHT: This 22-year-old male presents with acute onset (2-day) fever, altered mentation (confusion, disorientation), profuse sweating, and generalized rigidity — all occurring in the context of ongoing haloperidol therapy. Key red flags include hyperthermia (39.6°C), tachycardia (HR 116), leukocytosis (WBC 14,700/mm³), and markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK 5600 U/L), indicating significant muscle breakdown. Neurological exam shows rigidity but preserved limb movement, normal DTRs, and downgoing plantar responses — arguing against upper motor neuron lesion or primary encephalitis causing corticospinal tract signs. CSF is essentially normal (mildly elevated opening pressure, 4 WBCs — within non-inflammatory range; glucose and protein normal; no RBCs), making infectious meningitis/encephalitis highly unlikely. Brain MRI is unremarkable, further arguing against structural, inflammatory, or autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDA) as a primary cause — though early imaging can be normal in some encephalitides, the absence of seizures, headache, or focal neurology makes this less likely. Critically, the triad of fever, rigidity, and altered mental status — combined with autonomic instability (tachycardia, diaphoresis), elevated CK, and exposure to a dopamine D2 antagonist (haloperidol) — is classic for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). NMS typically develops over days (not hours), often with preserved consciousness early on (though confusion/disorientation are common), and does not require high-dose or recent dose escalation — even low-dose haloperidol can trigger it, especially in susceptible individuals. The absence of other explanatory causes (no infection on CSF/labs, no toxicology positives, no metabolic derangements reported, no evidence of serotonin syndrome — which would more likely feature myoclonus, hyperreflexia, clonus, diarrhea), and the temporal association with antipsychotic use strongly support NMS. While other conditions like malignant hyperthermia (MH) or heat stroke must be considered, MH is almost exclusively triggered by volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine — not applicable here — and heat stroke would lack rigidity and CK elevation out of proportion to clinical severity, and usually has multiorgan involvement not yet evident. Autoimmune encephalitis is less likely without CSF pleocytosis, MRI abnormalities, or seizure history. Thus, NMS is the most coherent, parsimonious, and urgent diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
